# Managing multiple AI coding agents from one list

Every agent you add is one more thing that can stop you in the middle of a thought. Managing multiple AI coding agents comes down to deciding, before the work starts, what is allowed to stop you.

Name the few moments that need a person. Everything else the agent settles alone, or it writes down what it needs and waits for you. Then what waits sits in one list, and you read it when you choose.

## Why supervision does not scale with the agents

Addy Osmani put the limit in one sentence in 2026. "What scales is your throughput of supervision, not your throughput of understanding." He gives his own number too. "My ceiling for a typical session is somewhere around three to four threads depending on complexity."

His advice is to narrow each agent's task before you cut the count. We agree. He also writes that an agent's judgment calls cannot queue up like email, and there we part. They cannot queue when any agent may ask anything at any time. They can when the flow says in advance which questions exist.

## Decide first which moments need a person

Tillerly runs AI coding agents on your team's machines, sandboxed, from ticket to pull request. Every ticket takes the same seven Steps, plan, publish, resolve, pull request, CI, QA and merge, and each Step blocks the next. One agent, the planner, designs the change. Another, the resolver, implements it. A person is needed at a short, fixed list of moments.

- The plan. The planner asks what it cannot decide alone, and the plan is implemented only when you say so.

- A question on the ticket. The resolver asks on your tracker and waits for whoever answers there.

- The pull request. Your team opens it. The agent never does.

- A comment that needs a decision. It waits for you.

- QA. When the build is green, QA waits for you.

- The merge. Your team merges on the code host.

Outside that list an agent has two choices. Settle it, or write down what it needs and wait. The Builder and its seven Steps says what each Step does.

## What an agent settles without you

The resolver implements the ticket in its own worktree, runs your repository's checks, and pushes the ticket's branch. None of that asks you anything.

Review works the same way, when the project's Follow comments setting is on. Within a few minutes of a new comment on the pull request, the resolver reads it and fixes what it can prove. A comment that comes while the build is red starts a fix of the build instead.

It leaves you the reply, ready to paste. A comment it cannot settle waits for you.

## One list of what waits

Each thing an agent needs from you becomes a human action. Open a pull request, reply to a reviewer, groom and start a bug, take a decision. They are all listed on Work, the dashboard's home.

Every open one is listed, none behind a second page, and the same open item is never added twice. So three agents asking are not three terminals to watch. They are three rows, read in one pass, at a stopping point of your own. You tick each one when it is done. What Work lists, and what your agents do meanwhile .

## A handoff you can check

A row only helps if you can act on it without replaying the agent's session. For a review comment, the human action says the pull request, the comment and its author, the verdict, why, and what you must do.

After a review session, the ticket shows what the session fixed and what it left you. You still read the diff. You are spared working out how the agent got there.

## Cap the agents at what you can review

The count is a setting, and it is yours. Each member chooses how many tickets they work at once, up to what the organization allows. Each ticket has its own resolver and its own folder on your machine. Our article on parallel agents and worktrees says how that folder is kept apart from the others.

Lower the number and the extra tickets wait until you raise it again. If three to four threads is your ceiling too, set it there.

## What it does not remove

- A person still reads every pull request. The list orders your attention and nothing more.

- A question that waits is a ticket that waits. The resolver waits on that ticket until someone answers. A list left unread is work standing still.

- One or two agents do not need this. A terminal each is enough, and you can watch both.

Your team still decides what is worked on, opens every pull request, does QA and merges. The agents work between those moments, and what they need from you is in one place.
